I am 55 years old, and I have farmed my land in Quzhou County since I was a young man. My father taught me how to read this soil, and after thirty-five years of working it myself, I know what it can do. I finished middle school, which was more than my father had, so I can read the seed bags and understand the fertilizer labels well enough. But experience is what I trust most.

It is April now, so my winter wheat is already in the ground from last October. I plant the same way every year: wheat in autumn, corn in summer. That is the rotation that works on the North China Plain, and I see no reason to change it. I have six mu of good flat land. I will put all six mu into winter wheat this season, and then the same six mu into summer corn after the harvest in early June.

For the wheat, I buy improved seed — last year I used Luyuan 502, and it did well, so I will use an improved variety like that again. I do not save my own wheat seed; the bought seed is cleaner and sprouts better. Before planting, I till the ground with a rotary tiller to break up the corn stubble and make a good seedbed. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer as my basal dose, and then I top-dress with urea when the wheat greens up after winter and again at jointing. I know my land needs nitrogen, and I have learned that about seventeen kilograms of nitrogen per mu gives me a solid crop, along with phosphate and some potash from the compound. I irrigate three times from my well — once when the wheat is reviving, once at jointing, and once at grain filling — because rain alone is never enough here. I also spray four times total: herbicide to control weeds, insecticide for aphids, and fungicide if I see rust starting. I expect about five hundred kilograms per mu from this wheat if the weather cooperates.

As soon as the wheat is harvested in early June, I will plant summer corn. I will buy Denghai 605 hybrid seed from the shop in town. It costs more, but the yield is worth it. I do not till the ground for the corn — I plant no-till straight into the wheat stubble to save time and keep the moisture. I put down compound fertilizer at planting, and that is usually enough for the corn, though sometimes I add a little urea if the plants look yellow. The corn needs two irrigations: one when it is young, and one during the big trumpet stage when it is shooting up. I spray herbicide once and insecticide two or three times, because the corn borer is a problem some years. If things go normally, I should get about six hundred and twenty-five kilograms per mu from the corn.

This is not fancy farming, but it is honest. Wheat and corn are what the market here wants, and it is what I know. I do not gamble on strange crops.
